provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.1.2.4 (Clean Session) and MQTT 5.0 sections 3.1.2.4 (Clean Start) and 3.1.2.11.2 (Session Expiry Interval).
reference_answer: In 3.1.1 one flag does everything (3.1.1 §3.1.2.4): with CleanSession=0 the server resumes or creates the session and both sides must store it after the disconnect, queuing further QoS 1/2 messages for the client's subscriptions; with CleanSession=1 the session is discarded and lasts only as long as the network connection. 5.0 splits this in two. Clean Start (5.0 §3.1.2.4) only governs connect time: Clean Start=1 means discard any existing session and start a new one, Clean Start=0 means resume it. How long state survives is set by the Session Expiry Interval property in seconds (5.0 §3.1.2.11.2). If it is absent or 0 the session ends when the network connection closes; a non-zero Session Expiry Interval makes client and server keep the state after the connection closes for that long; 0xFFFFFFFF means the session never expires. So to reproduce CleanSession=0, connect with Clean Start=0 plus a non-zero Session Expiry Interval (0xFFFFFFFF for open-ended storage); leaving the property out gives you a session that dies at disconnect. The server can override the interval in CONNACK (5.0 §3.2.2.3.2) and the client can change it on DISCONNECT (§3.14.2.2.2), but not from 0 to non-zero.

provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.2.2.3 (Connect Return code, Table 3.1) and MQTT 5.0 section 3.2.2.2 (Connect Reason Code, Table 3-1).
reference_answer: In 3.1.1 the CONNACK byte is a Connect Return code with only six defined values (3.1.1 §3.2.2.3): 0x00 accepted, then 0x01 to 0x05 refusals, where 0x05 means Connection Refused, not authorized; values 6-255 are reserved. A server that sends a non-zero return code must then close the network connection. In 5.0 the byte is a Connect Reason Code (5.0 §3.2.2.2) drawn from the shared reason-code table (5.0 §2.4): 0x00 Success, and failures start at 0x80. The same refusal arrives as 0x87 (135) Not authorized. Any code of 128 (0x80) or greater means the connection failed, and the server must close the connection after sending it. 3.1.1's other refusals map to 0x84 Unsupported Protocol Version, 0x85 Client Identifier not valid, 0x88 Server unavailable and 0x86 Bad User Name or Password, and 5.0 adds new ones such as 0x80 Unspecified error, 0x8A Banned, 0x95 Packet too large and 0x9C/0x9D for server redirection. Note that a 5.0 server MAY send this CONNACK (3.1.1 says SHOULD) and may simply close the connection instead. So map 3.1.1's 5 to 5.0's 0x87, and test for >= 0x80 rather than non-zero.

reference_answer: Your check is still right for 0x80 but incomplete. In 3.1.1 the SUBACK payload holds one return code per topic filter, in the same order as the SUBSCRIBE, and the only allowed values are 0x00, 0x01 and 0x02 (success with the granted maximum QoS) and 0x80 = Failure; anything else is reserved (3.1.1 §3.9.3). In 5.0 the list keeps the same one-per-filter ordering but holds reason codes (5.0 §3.9.3): 0x00-0x02 still mean Granted QoS 0-2, and 0x80 is Unspecified error, meaning the subscription was refused. 5.0 adds more refusal codes, e.g. 0x83 Implementation specific error, 0x87 Not authorized, 0x8F Topic Filter invalid, 0x91 Packet Identifier in use, 0x97 Quota exceeded, 0x9E Shared Subscriptions not supported, 0xA1 Subscription Identifiers not supported and 0xA2 Wildcard Subscriptions not supported. The general rule (5.0 §2.4) is that any reason code of 0x80 or greater indicates failure, so test code >= 0x80 rather than code == 0x80; that test is also correct for 3.1.1.

search_query: auth packet type 15 challenge response login
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 sections 2.2.1 (control packet types) and 5.4.1 (client authentication) and MQTT 5.0 sections 2.1.2 (control packet types), 4.12 (Enhanced authentication) and 4.12.1 (Re-authentication).
reference_answer: In 3.1.1, control packet type 15 is Reserved and forbidden (3.1.1 §2.2.1), and there is no challenge/response step: the CONNECT carries User Name and Password fields, and implementations may add TLS client certificates, LDAP/OAuth tokens or similar outside the protocol (3.1.1 §5.4.1). In 5.0, type 15 is AUTH, sent Client to Server or Server to Client (5.0 §2.1.2, §3.15). Enhanced authentication (5.0 §4.12) starts when the client includes an Authentication Method in the CONNECT (for example SCRAM-SHA-1), optionally with Authentication Data. If the server needs another round it sends AUTH with reason code 0x18 (Continue authentication) plus its data, the client answers with AUTH 0x18, and so on until the server sends CONNACK with reason code 0; the server can reject at any point: it MAY send a CONNACK of 0x80 or above (e.g. 0x8C Bad authentication method or 0x87 Not authorized) and MUST close the connection. Every AUTH and the successful CONNACK must repeat the same Authentication Method, and sending AUTH when CONNECT had none is a Protocol Error. After connecting, the client can re-authenticate by sending AUTH with 0x19 (Re-authenticate) (5.0 §4.12.1). 5.0 also allows a Password without a User Name, which 3.1.1 did not.

In 5.0 DISCONNECT is the final packet sent from the Client or the Server, and either side may send it before closing (5.0 §3.14). A server may only do so after it has sent a CONNACK with a reason code below 0x80; refusals at connect time still use CONNACK. After sending it the sender must close the network connection (5.0 §3.14.4).

provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.1.2.5 (Will Flag) and MQTT 5.0 section 3.1.3.2.2 (Will Delay Interval).
reference_answer: Yes. In 3.1.1 (§3.1.2.5) the Will Message is stored with the network connection and must be published when the network connection is closed by anything other than a DISCONNECT (I/O error, missed keep alive, protocol error, socket closed by the client); the server should publish will messages promptly, and the client gets no say in the timing, so every blip fires the will. In 5.0 the will belongs to the session, and the client can add a Will Delay Interval property in seconds (5.0 §3.1.3.2.2). The default is 0, meaning publish immediately. With a delay set, the server waits until the Will Delay Interval has passed or the session ends, whichever happens first. If the device reconnects to that session before the delay runs out, the server must not send the will at all (5.0 §3.1.3.2.2, §3.1.2.5). So set a Will Delay Interval longer than a typical outage and a Session Expiry Interval at least that long, since the will goes out anyway when the session ends. As in 3.1.1, a normal DISCONNECT (reason 0x00) deletes the will; 5.0 adds 0x04 Disconnect with Will Message to ask for it to be published.

Keep Alive is a 16-bit number of seconds (maximum 65,535, about 18 hours); if the client has nothing else to send it must send a PINGREQ within that interval. For your 300 s that means about 450 s of silence. A value of 0 disables the mechanism in both. The difference is who sets the value. A 3.1.1 server has to live with the client's number, although it may disconnect clients it judges inactive at any time. In 5.0 the server may return a Server Keep Alive in CONNACK, and the client must use it instead of the value it sent (5.0 §3.2.2.3.14), typically because the server wants to time out idle clients sooner. The 3.1.1 CONNACK has nowhere to put the generated ID, so the client never learns it. In 5.0 the clean-session restriction is gone, and the server MUST return the generated ID in the Assigned Client Identifier property of CONNACK (5.0 §3.2.2.3.7); it must not be in use by any other current session. Store it if you want to resume that session later. A 5.0 server rejecting an ID may send reason code 0x85 Client Identifier not valid before closing.

reference_answer: Not entirely as-is, but the core carries over: the QoS 2 exchange is the same four packets in both (3.1.1 §4.3.3, 5.0 §4.3.3). The sender assigns an unused Packet Identifier, sends PUBLISH with QoS 2 and DUP=0, and treats it as unacknowledged until PUBREC arrives. It then sends a PUBREL carrying the same Packet Identifier as the original PUBLISH and treats that as unacknowledged until PUBCOMP. It must not re-send the PUBLISH once it has sent the PUBREL. The receiver answers with PUBREC, acknowledges duplicates of that PUBLISH with PUBREC without delivering them again until PUBREL arrives, replies to PUBREL with PUBCOMP, and afterwards treats the identifier as new. The identifier becomes free for reuse once PUBCOMP is received. PUBREL's fixed-header flag bits are 0,0,1,0 in both (§3.6.1). What 5.0 changes: PUBREC, PUBREL and PUBCOMP carry a reason code and optional properties (5.0 §3.5.2), and a PUBREC with a reason code of 0x80 or greater ends the exchange (no PUBREL, identifier freed). It also stops message expiry once the PUBLISH has been sent and caps in-flight QoS 1/2 sends by the peer's Receive Maximum (5.0 §4.9). So keep the four-step core but add reason-code parsing and that early-exit branch.

provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN) and MQTT 5.0 section 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN).
reference_answer: Yes, this behaves the same in both versions (3.1.1 §3.3.1.3, 5.0 §3.3.1.3). A PUBLISH with RETAIN=1 and a zero-byte payload is processed normally by the server, so clients that currently have matching subscriptions receive it like any other message. In addition, any retained message with the same topic name must be removed, so future subscribers get no retained message for that topic. The empty message itself must not be stored as a retained message. Also identical: a PUBLISH with RETAIN=0 never stores, removes or replaces the retained message, so the clear only works with RETAIN=1. Small 5.0 differences around it: whether existing subscribers see RETAIN=1 on forwarded messages depends on the Retain As Published subscription option (3.1.1 always forwards with RETAIN=0), and a 5.0 server that advertised Retain Available=0 answers any RETAIN=1 publish with DISCONNECT 0x9A Retain not supported.

search_query: bridge loop prevention keep retain flag subscribe options
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 sections 3.8.3 (SUBSCRIBE payload) and 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN) and MQTT 5.0 section 3.8.3.1 (Subscription Options).
reference_answer:
In 3.1.1 each topic filter in SUBSCRIBE is followed by a Requested QoS byte (3.1.1 §3.8.3): bits 0-1 hold QoS 0, 1 or 2 and the upper 6 bits are reserved and must be zero, otherwise the packet is malformed and the connection is closed. There is nothing to stop echo, and when forwarding on an established subscription the server MUST set the RETAIN flag to 0 (3.1.1 §3.3.1.3). In 5.0 that byte becomes Subscription Options (5.0 §3.8.3.1):
- Bits 0-1: Maximum QoS.
- Bit 2, No Local: if 1, messages are never forwarded back to a connection whose ClientID equals the publishing connection's, so your bridge won't receive its own publications (it is a Protocol Error on a shared subscription).
- Bit 3, Retain As Published: if 1, forwarded messages keep the RETAIN flag they were published with; if 0 the flag is cleared as in 3.1.1.
- Bits 4-5, Retain Handling: 0 = send retained messages at subscribe, 1 = send them only if the subscription does not already exist, 2 = do not send them.
- Bits 6-7 are reserved.
The spec notes that No Local and Retain As Published are meant for bridging.

search_query: shared subscription share name vs each matching client
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.3.5 (PUBLISH actions) and MQTT 5.0 section 4.8.2 (Shared Subscriptions).
reference_answer: On 3.1.1 there is no load balancing: the server sends each application message to every client that has a matching subscription (3.1.1 §3.3.5), so all three workers get every job and you would have to partition topics yourself. 5.0 adds shared subscriptions (5.0 §4.8.2). Each worker subscribes to $share/{ShareName}/{filter}, e.g. $share/workers/jobs/#. The ShareName must be at least one character and must not contain /, + or #, and the rest is an ordinary topic filter. Each matching message is then sent to exactly one of the sessions in that share group; the server is free to choose which session receives each message, so round-robin is not guaranteed. Other share groups and normal subscribers to jobs/# still get their own copies. No retained messages are sent when a session joins a shared subscription. If a QoS 2 delivery is interrupted the server must finish it with the same client when it reconnects, while for QoS 1 it should send the message to another member if the original session ends. Check Shared Subscription Available in CONNACK first; a server without support answers with 0x9E Shared Subscriptions not supported.

provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 3.3.2.1 (Topic Name) and MQTT 5.0 section 3.3.2.3.4 (Topic Alias).
reference_answer: Not in 3.1.1: the Topic Name must be present as the first field of every PUBLISH variable header (3.1.1 §3.3.2.1), so the full string travels each time. 5.0 adds the Topic Alias PUBLISH property (5.0 §3.3.2.3.4), a Two Byte Integer chosen by the sender. To set a mapping, send a PUBLISH with the full topic name plus the alias; afterwards send that alias with a zero-length topic name and the receiver substitutes the stored name (a zero-length name without an alias is a Protocol Error, 5.0 §3.3.2.1). You can remap an alias by sending it again with a different topic name. Limits: an alias of 0 is not permitted. The client may use aliases only up to the Topic Alias Maximum the server returned in CONNACK (§3.2.2.3.8), and the server is bounded by the maximum the client sent in CONNECT (§3.1.2.11.5); if that property is absent or 0, no aliases may be sent in that direction. Mappings exist only within one network connection and must not be carried forward to a new one, so after reconnecting you resend the full topic. Client-to-server and server-to-client aliases are independent.

search_query: limit unacknowledged qos 1 2 messages in flight
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 4.3.2 (QoS 1 delivery) and MQTT 5.0 sections 4.9 (Flow Control) and 3.1.2.11.3 (Receive Maximum).
reference_answer: 3.1.1 has no protocol-level window: a sender is permitted to send further PUBLISH packets with different packet identifiers while it waits for acknowledgements (3.1.1 §4.3.2, §4.3.3), so the gateway has no protocol means to cap what the broker keeps in flight. 5.0 adds flow control (5.0 §4.9). Each side announces a Receive Maximum, the client in CONNECT (5.0 §3.1.2.11.3) and the server in CONNACK (§3.2.2.3.3). It is a Two Byte Integer, 0 is a Protocol Error, and if absent it defaults to 65,535. The peer keeps a send quota initialised to at most that value. Every QoS 1 or QoS 2 PUBLISH decrements it, while each PUBACK or PUBCOMP (or a PUBREC with a reason code of 0x80 or greater) increments it. Once the quota reaches zero the sender must stop sending QoS 1/2 PUBLISH packets until acknowledgements arrive; QoS 0 may continue and all other packets must still be processed. So the gateway sets Receive Maximum to 10. A broker that overruns it is in error, and the gateway can disconnect with 0x93 Receive Maximum exceeded (5.0 §3.3.4). The value is per network connection and is not part of the session state.

The only ceiling comes from the Remaining Length encoding: at most four bytes of 7-bit groups with a continuation bit, so the Remaining Length can reach 268,435,455 bytes (about 256 MB) (3.1.1 §2.2.3). 5.0 uses the same encoding as its Variable Byte Integer, so the absolute ceiling is unchanged at 268,435,455 bytes (5.0 §1.5.5, §2.1.4). What 5.0 adds is a Maximum Packet Size property, a Four Byte Integer counting the whole packet (fixed header plus Remaining Length). The client sends it in CONNECT (5.0 §3.1.2.11.4) and the server in CONNACK (5.0 §3.2.2.3.6); 0 or a duplicate is a Protocol Error, and if absent only the encoding limit applies. With your 4096-byte limit, the server must not send packets exceeding it. If a message for you is too large, the server must discard it without sending it and behave as if delivery had completed; for a shared subscription it may pick another member instead. Either side that still receives an oversized packet treats it as a Protocol Error and disconnects with reason code 0x95 Packet too large.

reference_answer: 3.1.1 gives a message no lifetime. For a CleanSession=0 session the server MUST store further QoS 1 and QoS 2 messages that match the client's subscriptions while it is disconnected (3.1.1 §3.1.2.4), and retained messages should be kept until a client deletes them (3.1.1 §4.1); any time limit is just broker administrative policy. 5.0 adds the Message Expiry Interval PUBLISH property (5.0 §3.3.2.3.3), a Four Byte Integer giving the message's lifetime in seconds. If that interval passes before the server has started onward delivery to a matching subscriber, the server must delete its copy of the message for that subscriber, so a device reconnecting after 60 s gets no stale command. If the property is absent, the message does not expire. When the server does forward it, the PUBLISH must carry the received value minus the time the message spent waiting in the server, so the receiver sees the remaining lifetime. Expired retained messages are discarded too (5.0 §3.3.1.3), and once a QoS 2 PUBLISH has been sent, expiry no longer cancels that exchange (5.0 §4.3.3). So publish each command with Message Expiry Interval = 60.

A client can also request Response Information in CONNACK to get a suggested response-topic root (5.0 §3.2.2.3.15).

search_query: bad packet protocol violation reason before closing
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 sections 4.8 (Handling errors) and 3.8.3 (SUBSCRIBE payload) and MQTT 5.0 section 4.13.1 (Malformed Packet and Protocol Errors).
reference_answer: In 3.1.1 the broker must treat that SUBSCRIBE as malformed and close the network connection, because any of its reserved bits being non-zero is an error (3.1.1 §3.8.3). More generally, unless stated otherwise, a receiver that encounters a protocol violation MUST close the network connection on which it received the offending packet (3.1.1 §4.8). There is no way to explain why: 3.1.1 has no server-sent DISCONNECT and no reason codes, so the client just sees the connection drop. In 5.0 the broker still MUST close the network connection on a Malformed Packet or Protocol Error (5.0 §4.13.1), but it SHOULD send a DISCONNECT containing a reason code before closing. It uses 0x81 Malformed Packet or 0x82 Protocol Error unless a more specific code exists, such as 0x93 Receive Maximum exceeded, 0x95 Packet too large or 0x9E Shared Subscriptions not supported. If the bad packet is the CONNECT, the server may send a CONNACK with the reason code before closing instead. Other errors can be reported per packet in 5.0 (§4.13.2): SUBACK, PUBACK and similar acks with a reason code of 0x80 or greater flag just that request and leave the connection up.

any: (?:\bbom\b|byte[- ]order mark|0xEF,? 0xBB,? 0xBF|u\+feff)(?:(?!(?<![\w.])3\.1\.1\b|\bmqtt[ -]?v?3\b|\bv3\b|\bversion\s+3\b)(?:[^.;]|\.(?=\S)|(?<=e\.g)\.|(?<=i\.e)\.)){0,40}(?:kept|preserved|retained|left in place|passed through|left alone|part of the string)

Both versions use a two-byte length prefix, so a string is at most 65,535 bytes.
5.0 keeps the 3.1.1 ban on U+0000 and on surrogate code points U+D800-U+DFFF.

search_query: string encoding null character surrogate byte order mark
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 section 1.5.3 (UTF-8 encoded strings) and MQTT 5.0 section 1.5.4 (UTF-8 Encoded String).
reference_answer: Yes, the string rules are the same in both (3.1.1 §1.5.3, 5.0 §1.5.4), so one encoder works. Each string has a two-byte length prefix, giving 0 to 65,535 bytes of character data. The data must be well-formed UTF-8 per RFC 3629. It must not include encodings of the surrogate code points U+D800 to U+DFFF, and it must not include the null character U+0000. Control characters U+0001-U+001F and U+007F-U+009F and Unicode non-characters SHOULD NOT be used, and a receiver may reject them. A 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF sequence is always interpreted as U+FEFF (zero width no-break space) wherever it appears and must not be skipped or stripped by the receiver. Only the error wording differs. In 3.1.1 a receiver that gets ill-formed UTF-8 or U+0000 MUST close the network connection, and it MAY close for the discouraged code points. In 5.0 those cases are a Malformed Packet handled under §4.13, so the receiver normally reports 0x81 Malformed Packet before closing, and the discouraged ones are called Disallowed Unicode code points (§5.4.9).

(?:topic )?level

A filter starting with a wildcard must not match topic names beginning with $.

search_query: multi-level single-level wildcard dollar topic matching
provenance: Facts come from MQTT 3.1.1 sections 4.7.1.2 (multi-level wildcard), 4.7.1.3 (single level wildcard) and 4.7.2 (topics beginning with $) and MQTT 5.0 sections 4.7.1.3 (single-level wildcard) and 4.7.2 (topics beginning with $).
reference_answer: Yes, topic matching is unchanged: the wildcard rules in 3.1.1 §4.7.1.2-§4.7.1.3 and §4.7.2 carry over essentially word for word into 5.0 under the same section numbers. The multi-level wildcard # matches any number of levels including the parent, so 'sport/#' also matches the bare 'sport'. It must stand alone or follow a '/', and it must be the last character of the filter, so 'sport/tennis#' and 'sport/tennis/#/ranking' are invalid. The single-level wildcard + matches exactly one level and must occupy an entire level, so 'sport/+' does not match 'sport' (it does match 'sport/'). Filters such as '+/tennis/#' combine both. For $ topics, the server must not match a filter that starts with a wildcard (# or +) against topic names beginning with $, so '#' never receives $SYS/... messages; subscribe to '$SYS/#' explicitly if you need them. The only 5.0 addition is the $share/{ShareName}/{filter} syntax for shared subscriptions (5.0 §4.8.2), whose {filter} part follows these same rules.
